hints: Focus on what the Avogadro constant actually counts, is it a mass in grams or a number of particles?
Remember that one mole of any substance always contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles.
Think about neon as single atoms, so one mole of neon must contain that exact number of atoms.
walkthrough:
**Recall what the Avogadro constant is**

Think of it as a counting number, just like a dozen means 12. It tells us how many particles are in one mole.

$$L = 6.02 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$$

**Separate number from mass**

Mass of one mole changes from element to element, that is the molar mass in g mol-1. The number per mole never changes, it is always the Avogadro constant.

**Apply to neon**

Neon exists as single atoms, $\text{Ne}$. So one mole of neon contains one mole of atoms, which is exactly the Avogadro number of atoms. That gives us our correct statement.

options.A: Incorrect. The mass of one mole is the molar mass, which is different for each element (e.g. about 20.2 g for neon, 12 g for carbon). The Avogadro constant is a number per mole, not a mass.
options.B: Incorrect. The mass of $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms is again the molar mass and depends on the element. The Avogadro constant itself is just the number $6.02 \times 10^{23}$, not a mass in grams.
options.C: Correct. By definition, one mole contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles. Since neon is monatomic, one mole of neon contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms, which is the Avogadro constant.
options.D: Incorrect. 12 g contains the Avogadro number of atoms only for carbon-12. For any other element, 12 g is not one mole, so it will not contain $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms.
